DuplicateFinder Pro — User Guide

How to scan your drives, decide what goes, and remove it without ever putting a file at risk. Written for the way photographers and videographers actually store their work.

Start here

DuplicateFinder Pro finds files you are storing more than once and helps you remove the extra copies. It is built around one promise, and everything else in the app follows from it.

Nothing is ever deleted without you asking twice.

When you remove a duplicate, the file is moved to a quarantine folder on its own drive, inside the folder you scanned. It stays there, and Restore Selected on the Quarantine tab puts it back, until you personally choose to delete it — and even then, not for the first 24 hours.

That means you can explore freely. Scan a drive, flag things, move them to quarantine, change your mind. Nothing you do in this app is irreversible until you deliberately make it so.

The screenshots in this guide come from a real session. Click any of them to see it full size, and click again or press Esc to close it.

What counts as a duplicate

The app compares files by their content, not their names. Two files with completely different filenames, in different folders, on different drives, are still duplicates if their bytes are identical. Equally, two files with the same name are not duplicates if their contents differ. A RAW and the JPG made from it are never the same file, so they are never duplicates of each other. The two RAW+JPG tabs treat them as a pair instead — and only when the JPG still has the RAW's name.

The free version and the licensed version

Without a license you can scan, review results, and export both reports. Moving files to quarantine requires a license key, which you enter under Help → Enter License Key… — the key is on your purchase receipt.

The screen at a glance

The window has three areas, and it is worth learning which is which before your first scan.

The left sidebar — settings and actions

Everything on the left applies to the scan as a whole. Browse… picks the folder to scan. Beneath it, RAW/JPG Similarity Threshold applies to the RAW+JPG Cross-Folder tab only. There, a JPG with the same name as a RAW must also look like it: lower values accept heavier crops and edits, higher values only near-identical exports. It never makes files with different names into a pair. Below that, What Gets Scanned lets you switch whole categories of file on and off.

The action buttons live at the bottom of the sidebar: starting, pausing and stopping a scan, Reset, the two quarantine buttons, and the two report exports.

Reset clears every result, flag and keeper choice on every tab and puts the app back the way it opened. It asks before it does anything, and it never touches files already in quarantine.

The tabs — your results

Each tab holds one kind of finding, and each carries a pair of numbers.

Duplicate JPGs (45 / 87)

45 flagged for removal, out of 87 found

Read it as a fraction: this many of that many. The second number is how many items the scan found. The first is how many of them are currently marked to be removed, and it changes as you work — flag more files and it rises, make one a keeper instead and it falls.

So a first number of 0 means the scan found things and you have decided to remove none of them, while two matching numbers, such as (53 / 53), mean everything found is flagged. The WAV Audio tab shows both extremes in ordinary use: on a camera card dump every WAV is usually flagged, and on a folder of music none is — see WAV Audio.

Watch the first number before you press a quarantine button. It is the count of files that will actually move.

The row buttons — the bar along the bottom

These act on whatever is highlighted in the list above them. They change what you have decided about specific files; they do not move anything.

Getting the tips back

The first time you run the app it walks you through the basics with small pop-up tips. If you closed them and want them again, they are not gone: Help → Show Getting-Started Tips Again brings them back, as many times as you like. It picks up at the tip for where you are: the first one if no folder is chosen yet, the scan tip if a folder is chosen, and the last one if results are already on screen. The tips remind you of this menu entry themselves when you turn them off.

Your first scan

If you are trying the app for the first time, point it at one folder rather than an entire drive. A single shoot or a single year is enough to see how everything behaves, and it finishes in minutes instead of hours.

  1. Choose what to scan

    Click Browse… at the top of the sidebar and pick a folder. Everything beneath it is scanned, however deep the folders go.

  2. Choose what to look for

    Under What Gets Scanned, tick the categories that matter to you. If you only care about photographs, turn video off — the scan will be considerably faster.

  3. Start the scan

    Click Start Scan. The status line under the results shows which phase it is in and how far along it is. Indexing comes first — finding every file — then RAW/JPG pairing, then the duplicate checks for JPGs, RAWs and videos.

    Phase 3: Duplicate JPG detection…

  4. Look through the tabs

    As results arrive, the tab labels fill in with counts. Click through them. Selecting any row shows a preview underneath, so you can see what you are about to decide on.

  5. Decide what stays

    The app pre-selects a keeper in each group and flags the rest. Review those choices and adjust them using the buttons along the bottom — see Keeping and flagging.

  6. Move the flagged files to quarantine

    Use one of the two quarantine buttons in the sidebar. A confirmation appears first, telling you exactly how many files will move and how much space they take up.

  7. Check the results, then delete for real

    Open the Quarantine tab, confirm the right things are in there, and wait. After 24 hours the permanent delete unlocks. Before and after that, Restore Selected puts anything straight back where it came from.

The tabs, one by one

RAW+JPG Same Folder

RAW files with a JPG of the same name beside them in the same folder — IMG_0412.CR3 and IMG_0412.JPG. That is what a camera writes when it shoots RAW+JPG. If you keep your RAW originals and re-export whenever you need a JPG, these JPGs are redundant. If you hand JPGs to clients straight out of this folder, they are not — which is why nothing here is removed automatically.

RAW+JPG Cross-Folder

The same relationship, but where the JPG lives somewhere else entirely — an exports folder, a delivery folder, an old backup. The JPG must still have the RAW's name, and because camera numbering repeats across cards and years, a shared name is not enough here: each pair is also compared image to image before it is flagged. This is the tab that finds the copies you forgot you made.

Renamed exports are never paired. If you export DSCF0244.RAF as BoatCruise_023.jpg, neither tab links the two. That is deliberate: a renamed, edited JPG is usually a finished picture, not a spare copy, and the app will not guess otherwise.

WAV Audio

Every WAV file the scan found. Some cameras record a separate audio file beside each clip — a GoPro writes GH010042.WAV next to GH010042.MP4 — and once the video is safely kept, that audio copy is usually surplus. The app recognises it by where it sits, not by brand: a WAV in the same folder as a video with the same name is treated as that video's audio sidecar and flagged for you. The same rule covers other cameras and formats, including Sony .MTS and .MXF and Canon .CRM clips.

Any other WAV — music, a live recording, a voice memo — is listed so you can see it, but kept unless you flag it yourself. The Status column says which is which, and clicking a row spells out the reason on the line under the table:

StatusMeaning
⚠ SidecarA video with the same name sits beside it. Flagged automatically.
? Possible sidecarNo matching video beside it, but some sign it belongs to one (see below). Shown in amber and left for you to decide; never flagged for you.
✓ Kept — no videoNo matching video beside it and nothing else suggesting one, so the app leaves it alone.
✓ Kept — your decisionYou kept it with ✓ Keep Selected. ↺ Reset Selected hands it back to the app's own verdict.
✗ FlaggedNo matching video, but you flagged it yourself.

Results loaded from a session saved by an older version show ⚠ Auto-flag instead. Those were made before this rule existed, when every WAV was flagged; rescan to apply it.

Possible sidecars

Renaming files on import, or copying the audio into a different folder from its clips, breaks the same-name, same-folder test, so the app can no longer be sure. Instead of guessing, it marks the WAV ? Possible sidecar when any of these is true:

  • Its own recording information names a video clip. Many cameras store the clip's name inside the WAV. A GoPro WAV renamed to 20260530_GoPro11A_0093.WAV may still say it belongs to GX010239.MP4. You can see this yourself in Windows: right-click the file, Properties, Details, Title.
  • A video with the same name is somewhere else in the scan.
  • Its folder holds videos, just none with its name.

Click the row to see which applies, or rest the mouse on its Status for the same reason in a pop-up. A possible sidecar is not counted in the space total and is never moved until you flag it with ✗ Flag for Deletion. If it is a recording you want, ✓ Keep Selected makes that your decision: the row reads ✓ Kept — your decision and the suggestion goes away. ↺ Reset Selected brings it back.

Duplicate JPGs · Duplicate RAWs · Duplicate Videos

Straightforward content matches within each file type: the same photograph or the same clip, stored in more than one place. Each group shows one keeper and one or more duplicates, with a header line saying how many copies were found and how much removing the extras saves.

The Match column says how each copy was matched. md5 means the file contents were read and are identical. stem+size means the same name and a similar size, nothing more. On Duplicate RAWs, Review marks copies whose sizes differ by more than 5% — probably different versions of the same shot — so look before you decide.

Duplicate Videos compares whole file contents only, never a single frame or thumbnail. Two chapters of one continuous GoPro recording are therefore never mistaken for copies of each other.

Quarantine

Everything you have moved, with the folder each file came from and when the 24-hour hold expires. Covered in full below.

Folder Duplicates

A different kind of comparison: whole folders or whole drives against each other. Covered in full below.

Storage Map

A pie chart of where your space is actually going. Each slice is a folder, sized by how much it holds, and every folder keeps the same colour wherever it appears so you can follow it as you move around.

Click a slice to drill into that folder and see its own contents broken down the same way. ◀ Back returns one level, ⌂ Root jumps all the way out. The strip along the top shows the total for the level you are looking at and, once a scan has run, how much space your scans could recover.

Drill down far enough and you reach individual files, listed with a tick box beside each one. Ticking files here adds them to the same flagged set the sidebar's Move Flagged to Quarantine button acts on — so the map is not just a picture, it is somewhere you can work. Right-click any file for Open / Show in Explorer, Copy Full Path, and the tick and untick commands.

Calculating folder sizes across a large drive takes time. A ✕ Cancel Calculation button appears while it runs, and 🔄 Refresh recalculates when you want current numbers.

The recoverable figure covers everything your scans found, not just the folder on screen, and it always matches the header. After a main scan alone it reads like Recoverable: 112.6 GB (46.4% of this folder). Once a Folder Duplicates comparison adds to it, the line splits the figure by where it comes from — Recoverable: 2.3 TB = main scan 112.7 GB + Folder Duplicates 2.2 TB — and a line underneath explains that the Folder Duplicates part lives in the folders compared on that tab. Those can be whole other drives, which this map does not show, so the total can be larger than the folder on screen without anything being wrong.

The map charts the folder you scanned in the sidebar, so it fills in after a main scan. A Folder Duplicates scan on its own leaves it empty, and so does loading a session that only holds Folder Duplicates results.

Use this after a scan rather than before. It is the fastest way to find the handful of folders responsible for most of your drive, which are usually where the worthwhile duplicates are hiding.

Settings & Profiles

Saved combinations of scan settings. If you scan card dumps one way and archive drives another, save each as a profile rather than re-adjusting the sidebar each time.

The same tab holds Folder Exclusions — folders the scan skips entirely — and your saved sessions, covered below. A useful habit: once you have finished with a folder in Folder Duplicates, exclude it here so a full-drive scan does not go over it again.

Keeping and flagging

Every duplicate group has exactly one keeper — the copy that survives — and one or more flagged files, which are the ones that will move when you quarantine. The app chooses for you, and you can overrule it.

ButtonWhat it does
✓ Keep SelectedMakes the highlighted file the keeper for its group. Whichever file was previously the keeper becomes flagged instead. On the three Duplicate tabs it reads ✓ Mark Selected as Keeper.
✗ Flag for DeletionMarks the highlighted files for removal. A group always keeps one copy, so you cannot flag every file in a group. On the three Duplicate tabs it reads ✗ Flag Selected for Deletion.
Select AllHighlights every row on the current tab, for use with the buttons around it.
↺ Reset SelectedPuts the highlighted rows back to what the scan originally decided, undoing your own changes to them.
View Scan LogFolder Duplicates only. Opens the detailed record of what the scan did, including anything it skipped and why.
Copy SummaryFolder Duplicates only. Puts a short text summary of the result on your clipboard.

None of these buttons move or delete anything. They only change what the app intends to do when you press one of the quarantine buttons.

To swap which copy survives, highlight the one you want to keep and press ✓ Keep Selected. You do not need to flag the other one separately — that happens as a consequence.

The quarantine buttons

There are two of them in the sidebar and they are genuinely different. Confusing them is the most common way people move more than they meant to.

ButtonActs onUse it when
Move Flagged to Quarantine Every flagged file on the tab you are currently looking at. You have reviewed the whole tab and you are happy with all of it.
Move Selected to Quarantine Only the rows you have highlighted, and nothing else. You want to work through a large result set in pieces, or take a handful of files now and decide on the rest later.

Why "Flagged" is narrower than it sounds

Move Flagged to Quarantine is scoped to the active tab only. Standing on the Duplicate JPGs tab, it moves flagged JPGs and leaves your flagged videos exactly where they are. It never sweeps every category at once. The same command appears under Quarantine → Move Flagged to Quarantine in the menu bar and behaves identically.

The button is greyed out on the Quarantine, Folder Duplicates and Settings tabs, because the action has no meaning there. Folder Duplicates has its own pair of quarantine buttons along the bottom of that tab.

Which one to reach for

If a tab shows you a few dozen results you have read through, use Move Flagged to Quarantine. If it shows you thousands, use Move Selected to Quarantine and work down in batches you can actually check. Both buttons carry their counts — Move 36 Flagged to Quarantine, Move 1 Selected to Quarantine — and a confirmation always appears first, with the file count and the space involved, so you get one more chance to look before anything moves.

Quarantine never crosses drives

Each file goes to a _DuplicateFinder_Quarantine folder inside the folder it was scanned from, on its own drive. Windows only has to update where the file is listed, so the move is instant whatever the size, and it needs no free space. That holds even when a Folder Duplicates comparison spans several drives: a file on D: stays on D:, a file on H: stays on H:.

Why quarantining can still take a while

On the Folder Duplicates tab, every flagged file is re-read in full alongside its keeper just before it moves, to confirm the two are still identical. That check is what the progress notice is counting — "2.9 GB of 3.3 GB read (both copies)" is reading, not copying — and on large video files it takes time. It is there so that a file that changed since the scan is never removed on the strength of an old comparison. The move itself is instant.

Inside the Quarantine tab

This tab lists everything you have moved, where it originally lived, and when its hold expires. Three buttons act on it.

ButtonWhat it does
🔄 Restore SelectedPuts the highlighted files back in their original folders. Available at any time, hold or no hold.
🗑 Permanently Delete SelectedDeletes only the highlighted files, once their individual holds have expired.
🗑 Permanently Delete AllDeletes everything past its hold. While anything is still held, the button reads (24h lock) and files still inside their window are left alone.

Each row shows the file, which tab it came from, its size, when it was quarantined, and — under Deletes After — when its hold ends and permanent deletion becomes possible. Nothing is deleted automatically at that time; it only becomes something you can do. The last column is the folder Restore Selected puts it back into.

The 24-hour hold

Every quarantined file carries a timestamp, and for 24 hours from that moment it cannot be permanently deleted. The hold exists for one specific risk: discovering the next morning that the copy you kept was the wrong one. A day is long enough to notice, and short enough not to be in the way.

The hold is per file, not per batch. Files moved on Monday unlock on Tuesday regardless of what you moved on Wednesday.

Quarantined files stay on disk and keep occupying space until you permanently delete them. Moving files to quarantine does not free space on its own — it makes the removal reversible. The space comes back at the permanent delete.

So that held files are not forgotten, the app reminds you when it opens if any of them are past their hold: how many, how much space they take, and an offer to open this tab. Files still inside their hold never trigger a reminder, because there is nothing to do about them yet.

Folder Duplicates

The other tabs look inside one folder tree for duplicated media. This tab compares two or more places against each other, and it works differently in two important ways.

Add folders or whole drives with + Add Folder / Drive…, then press Scan for Duplicate Files.

It compares everything, not just photos and video

Every file under each folder you add is checked by content against every file under the others, at any depth, regardless of type. Documents, archives, application files, anything. The What Gets Scanned settings in the sidebar do not apply here.

That is deliberate and it is often exactly what you want on an old backup drive. It also means that on a drive holding old computer backups or installed software, it will correctly identify the shared files inside those programs as duplicates of each other. They are real duplicates, but they belong to software, and removing them can break it. Their count is often large while their size is tiny, so review by folder rather than quarantining a whole-drive result in one go.

The order of your folders decides who wins

The copy in the first folder in the list is the keeper. Matching copies in every folder below it are the ones flagged. Where two copies sit under the same folder, the one with the shorter path is kept.

To change which copy survives, select a folder in the list and use ▲ Move Up or ▼ Move Down. Every group's keeper is re-assigned straight away from the new order — no rescan — and the status line reports how many groups changed and which folder now wins. The recoverable total and the header update with it.

Reordering applies the rule afresh, so a keeper you chose by hand with ✓ Keep Selected is replaced by whatever the new order says. Settle the order first, then make individual choices.

Be careful with backup drives

If you add both your working drive and your backup drive, every file that exists on both is a match — and the copy on whichever drive you listed second is what gets flagged. That is your backup. The app cannot tell a wasteful duplicate from a deliberate second copy; only you can. Either leave backup drives out of the comparison, or list the backup first so it becomes the keeper.

When a file is also on another tab

A file can appear here and on one of the main scan's tabs at the same time, and the two can disagree: flagged here as a redundant copy, but kept on another tab as the RAW of a RAW+JPG pair, for example. Both can be right, because each tab asks a different question. The Match column tells you when it happens: md5 · also in Dup RAWs, or md5 · keeper in WAV when another tab is keeping the file. Click the row and the line under the preview says which tabs, and what each one decided; resting the mouse on the Match cell shows the same in a pop-up. Quarantining a file here removes it from those tabs too, and the confirmation counts how many of the files you are moving are affected.

Working through a large result

Comparing whole drives can produce results in the hundreds of thousands. Most of the recoverable space usually sits in a small number of large groups, so sort before you scroll. Click a column heading to sort; click it again to reverse. Sorting always moves whole groups, so a keeper never gets separated from the copies it protects.

HeadingSorts groups by
SizeHow much space removing the group's flagged copies would free — the "Save" figure in each group header — largest first. While active the heading reads Size · by space saved. This is why a group of two 4 GB files can sit below a group of five 2.6 GB files: 8 GB saved against 13 GB.
FileFile name, A to Z.
FolderThe folder of the flagged copy — the folder a cleanup would empty — so groups sitting in the same place end up together.
RoleNumber of copies, most first.

Sorts can be combined. Groups that tie keep the order they already had, so sorting by Size and then by Folder gives you the groups arranged folder by folder, with the biggest savings first inside each one. For work outside the app, the CSV report holds every row and opens in Excel.

Reports you can keep

Export Report (CSV)

A complete row-by-row record: every group, every file, which copy is the keeper, which are flagged, and the size of each. This is the file to keep if you want a record of what you removed, or if you want to sort and filter results outside the app.

Export Summary (HTML)

A single readable page that opens in any browser. It contains:

  • The estimated recoverable space, split by drive — and within each drive, how much comes from the main scan and how much from Folder Duplicates. The rows add up to the figure in the app's header.
  • A section for the main scan — what was scanned, when it started and finished, scanning time with pauses left out, the files examined by type, and every category's found, flagged and recoverable figures.
  • A section for Folder Duplicates — the folders compared, in order, with the keeper marked; the same timing and file counts; and how much of its flagged space the main scan already counts, so nothing is counted twice.
  • Quarantine — files held, their size, and how many are past the 24-hour hold.

A scan that was stopped and resumed reports its first start time and the working time of every run added together. The Print / Save as PDF button at the top opens your browser's print dialog; choose Save as PDF or Microsoft Print to PDF for a file. Printed, the page switches to plain black on white.

Timing and file counts are recorded from v1.6 on. A report made from a session saved by an earlier version shows the results with a short note in place of those details.

Both exports are available without a license, and neither changes anything on disk.

If a Folder Duplicates scan is still running when you export, the app stops to warn you: its results are not ready yet, so the report would come out with that section empty. Let the scan finish, then export.

Saving and loading sessions

Save Current Session on the Settings & Profiles tab keeps everything on screen: the main scan's results and the Folder Duplicates comparison, including every keep and flag decision you have made in both. The app also saves automatically when you close it, and offers that back next time you open it.

Loading a session replaces both halves with whatever that session holds. A session saved with only Folder Duplicates results brings back an empty main scan, and the other way round. Your quarantine is never taken from a session — it is always read fresh from what is actually in quarantine.

Keeping both scans in one session

  1. Load the session holding the result you want to keep.
  2. Run the other scan. Starting a main scan does not clear Folder Duplicates results, and both scans reuse each other's already-checked files, so this is quick.
  3. Save the session. That one file now holds both.

The app will not let you save a session with nothing in it, and if you load one saved empty by an earlier version it tells you so, so it is safe to delete.

Long scans, pausing, stopping

A scan across several full drives can run for hours. Three things make that survivable.

Pause and resume

Pause Scan stops the work and lets the drives go idle, which is what you want if you need the machine's full speed for something else. Resume Scan picks up from the same position. Nothing is lost and nothing is re-read.

Stopping and coming back later

Every file the app has content-checked is remembered, shared between both kinds of scan, and kept after you close the app. Rescanning the same files is therefore fast whichever scan checked them first.

A Folder Duplicates scan goes further. Once it has finished listing the folders, it saves that list. If you then stop it — or close the app, or the computer restarts — the scan button reads ▶ Resume Scan the next time you have the same folders listed, with ↻ Start Fresh beside it:

  • Resume Scan picks up where it left off — no re-listing, and nothing already checked is read again. The status line shows when the stopped scan was saved and how many files it holds.
  • Start Fresh throws the saved list away and walks every folder again.

The saved list is a snapshot. Files deleted or changed since you stopped are handled safely — they are left out rather than matched on old information — but files added since are not seen until you choose Start Fresh. Resume also refuses to run while one of the compared drives is unplugged, because it would silently leave out everything on it; reconnect the drive, or start fresh with what is connected.

A scan stopped before listing finished has nothing to resume from, and says so. Changing the folder order with Move Up / Move Down does not affect resuming.

If you are in another window when it finishes

When a scan finishes while you are working in something else, the app’s taskbar button flashes and Windows plays its notification sound. The flashing stops when you switch back. If the app was already in front of you, nothing happens — you can see it finished.

One scan at a time

The main scan and a Folder Duplicates scan cannot run at the same time — they share the same record of checked files and the same drives. Starting one while the other is running asks you to let it finish or stop it first. Stopping costs nothing, since a stopped Folder Duplicates scan can be resumed.

Your computer will not fall asleep mid-scan

While a scan is running the app asks Windows to stay awake, so a long unattended run finishes instead of stalling. Your monitor still sleeps normally.

What the app never touches

  • Windows system folders and program installation folders are excluded from scanning and can never be flagged, whichever drive they happen to sit on.
  • Windows File History folders are excluded too. Windows keeps and prunes those backup versions itself, and removing copies from them file by file would break its restore history.
  • Quarantine never moves a file to another drive.
  • The quarantine folder itself is excluded, so quarantined files are never re-detected as duplicates of the originals they came from.
  • A group always retains one copy. There is no sequence of clicks that flags every copy of a file.
  • Nothing is deleted by a scan. Scanning only reads.

Questions we get asked

I closed the getting-started tips. How do I get them back?

Help → Show Getting-Started Tips Again. It shows the tip for the point you have reached, and you can do it as often as you want.

Where do quarantined files actually go?

Into a folder named _DuplicateFinder_Quarantine, created at the top of the folder the file was scanned from, on the file's own drive. Compare whole drives in Folder Duplicates and you will find one on each — D:\_DuplicateFinder_Quarantine, H:\_DuplicateFinder_Quarantine and so on. You can open them in File Explorer like any other folder, though restoring through the app is safer because it puts each file back in its original location.

Why does quarantining take time if nothing is copied?

Folder Duplicates re-reads each flagged file against its keeper just before moving it, to be certain they still match. The notice shows that reading as it happens. The move itself is instant. See The quarantine buttons.

Why does the WAV Audio tab show 0 flagged?

None of those WAVs has a video with the same name beside it, so none is flagged for you. That is the right answer for a music collection. Any that show ? Possible sidecar in amber are ones the app thinks may belong to a video; click one to see why, and flag it yourself if it can go. See WAV Audio.

Why does a tab show a number like 45 / 87?

45 files currently flagged for removal, out of 87 the scan found. Read it as a fraction — the first number is the one that moves when you quarantine.

The Storage Map says more is recoverable than the folder holds.

The recoverable figure is for everything your scans found, including any Folder Duplicates comparison of other drives. The folder total is only the folder on screen. Both numbers are right; they answer different questions. The Storage Map splits the figure into its main-scan and Folder Duplicates parts, so you can see which one is outside the folder. See Storage Map.

The scan found a file type I did not ask for.

You were almost certainly on the Folder Duplicates tab, which compares every file by content regardless of type. The What Gets Scanned list applies to the other tabs.

I quarantined files but my free space did not change.

Expected. Quarantine moves files, it does not delete them. Space is recovered when you permanently delete them after the hold expires.

Can I delete something before the 24 hours are up?

No, and that is the point of the hold. You can restore it immediately, or wait out the window.

Is a scan safe to leave running overnight?

Yes. The app keeps the computer awake, and a scan only ever reads your files.

A message said my text size was adjusted to fit the screen.

Windows display scaling enlarges text, and on some screens — a 1920 × 1080 laptop at 150%, for example — the window at full enlargement would be wider than the display. Rather than run off the edge, the app uses the largest text size that still fits everything, and tells you once. The text is a little smaller than Windows asked for, but sharp, and every button is reachable. On a larger or higher-resolution screen the full size is used and the message never appears.

You can make text larger again in Windows Display settings, though part of the window may then sit off-screen. If the left-hand column is taller than your screen, a scroll bar appears beside it.

The app looks slightly soft on my second monitor.

The app draws itself for your main display. If a second monitor uses different scaling, Windows resizes the whole window evenly when you move it there — slightly soft, but the right size and never cut off. Dragging it back makes it crisp again.

Can I scan my phone directly?

Not reliably. iPhones do not let desktop programs see their files at all, and Android phones connected by cable use a slow connection that tends to drop partway through a long scan. Scan the folder you import your phone photos into instead — that is also where duplicates actually pile up, because the same import gets made twice far more often than a phone stores the same photo twice.

You can see why in File Explorer, under This PC. A connected iPhone appears beside your drives, but it is a different kind of thing: it has no drive letter and no bar showing free space, because Windows cannot read its storage directly. It has to ask the phone for each file in turn, which is also why that view can be slow to fill in.

So an iPhone will not show up in Browse… at all. If you type a phone's name into the scan box instead, or pick a camera or an Android phone that Windows lists as a folder but won't let the app read, the app says so: straight away, if what you chose is not a real folder, or when a scan finds no files at all. A camera's memory card in a card reader is different: it gets a drive letter and scans like any other drive.

Getting help

Everything below is in the Help menu inside the app.

  • User Guide (or press F1) — this guide, as installed with the app. Works offline. It is also in the Windows Start menu, under Almaze.
  • User Guide (Online — latest) — the same guide on the Almaze website, which is updated first.
  • Send Feedback / Suggest a Feature — tell us what is missing. Features get built from these.
  • Report a Bug — include what you were doing and what you expected instead. A screenshot helps more than anything else: drag an image into the report, or paste one with Ctrl+V. Rename or blur any personal folder names first. Both this and the feedback link open a page on GitHub, which needs a free GitHub account. If you would rather not create one, email support@almaze.tools instead — replying to your purchase receipt reaches the same address — and attach the screenshot there.
  • Show Getting-Started Tips Again — replays the first-run walkthrough.
  • Enter License Key… — the key from your purchase receipt.
  • About DuplicateFinder Pro — the version and build you are running. Quote these when you write to us; it is the fastest way for us to know what you are looking at.
